children: Oil prices rose in early European trading Thursday, with Brent holding above $100 a barrel after Wednesday's sharp rally as markets assessed escalating attacks on Gulf shipping and renewed Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia.

Front-month Brent crude oil futures gained 0.2% to $101.36 a barrel, while front-month West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures rose 0.3% to $96.36 a barrel. Both benchmarks traded mixed earlier in the Asian day after settling Wednesday at their highest closing levels since May 22.

U.S. Central Command said earlier this week that American forces had destroyed eight Iranian tankers in recent days, in response to fresh attempts by Tehran to strike U.S. warships in the Middle East.
Separately, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Center said Wednesday it had received reports of several merchant vessels being subjected to fire in the northern Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard warned on Wednesday of further restrictions on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz as Tehran seeks to challenge a U.S. naval blockade that has sharply curtailed its ability to export oil.
Meanwhile, a coalition led by Saudi Arabia pledged a response after another round of Houthi attacks on the kingdom Wednesday.
The persistence of the disruption is pushing analysts to extend their expectations for a tight market.

HSBC analyst Kim Fustier said Thursday that the oil market is unlikely to rebalance until mid-2027, with flows through Hormuz expected to rise from around 6 million barrels a day currently to 8 million by year-end and 9.5 million by mid-2027, still well below the prewar level of 19 million to 20 million barrels a day. HSBC raised its 2026 Brent forecast to $90 from $80 a barrel, while seeing prices around $120 in a prolonged-stalemate scenario.

Physical crude markets are showing even greater strain. S&P Global Commodity Insights said Platts Dated Brent, a benchmark for the spot-market value of physical crude, surged to $114.26 a barrel Wednesday, while Middle East Gulf sour-crude exports averaged 5.88 million barrels a day in the second quarter, down 65% from a year earlier. Tanker costs also surged, with the cost of shipping crude from the Arabian Gulf to the Far East on very large crude carriers reaching a record high Wednesday as security risks and uncertainty over shipping routes intensified.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration also raised its assessment of the disruption in its September outlook released Wednesday. It estimated Middle East crude-production shut-ins averaged 6.7 million barrels a day in August, up from 5 million in July, and expects shut-ins to average 5.7 million barrels a day in the fourth quarter. The agency said most production and trade flows may not return to preconflict averages until the second quarter of 2027.
